 WASHINGTON, D.C. (7News) — A proposal to raise Washington, D.C.‘s minimum wage to $25 an hour is moving closer to a possible ballot fight, setting up a new debate over worker pay, business costs and the future of the District’s hospitality industry.
 Supporters say the increase would help workers keep up with the rising cost of living . But business owners warn the proposal could lead to fewer jobs, reduced hours and higher prices for customers.
 Known as Initiative 87, the proposal would gradually increase D.C.’s current $18.40 minimum wage to $25 an hour by July 2029. It would also eliminate the lower base wage for tipped workers by July 2031.
 SEE ALSO | DC unions rally for pay increase as councilmembers weigh pay hike for new mayor 
 The proposal would affect employers across the District, not just restaurants. Retailers, hotels, childcare providers and other businesses employing minimum-wage workers could also face higher labor costs.
 What would Initiative 87 change?
 Under current law, D.C.‘s standard minimum wage is $18.40 an hour. Tipped employees have a lower base wage of $10.30 an hour, but employers must make up the difference if an employee’s wages and tips do not reach the full minimum wage.
 If approved by voters, Initiative 87 would gradually increase the standard minimum wage to $25 an hour by July 2029.
 The measure would also phase out the separate tipped minimum wage, bringing tipped employees to the same base minimum wage as other workers by July 2031, with tips on top.
 Another provision would require businesses to give employees service charges collected from customers.
 The proposal is not limited to the restaurant industry. It could affect private employers throughout the District, although the initiative includes exemptions for District government employees and workers employed by private contractors performing services under D.C. government contracts.
 Business owners warn of potential job losses and higher prices
 A new business opposition coalition, called No I-87, launched this week with backing from the Restaurant Association of Metropolitan Washington .
 The coalition argues that a rapid increase in labor costs could force employers to make difficult decisions, including reducing staffing, cutting employee hours or raising prices.
 Shawn Townsend, president and CEO of the Restaurant Association of Metropolitan Washington, said the industry wants employees to earn good wages but questions whether businesses can absorb the proposed increases.
 SEE ALSO | Inflation pressures spread across economy as prices continue to outpace wages 
 “Look, we want our hospitality workers to earn good wages and have opportunities to grow and build careers in this business. But Initiative 87, it isn’t just simply about raising wages, it’s whether or not D.C. restaurants can sustain under this pressure, whether or not we can keep those jobs, and keep those neighborhood businesses alive,” Townsend said. The opposition campaign says it is working to bring retailers, childcare providers, hotels and other industries into the debate.
 Supporters say workers need a more reliable paycheck
 Supporters, including One Fair Wage, argue that workers should be able to earn a dependable wage without relying on tips to make ends meet.
 The organization says the proposal would help workers keep pace with the District’s high cost of living and provide more predictable income for employees in tipped occupations.
 The measure has also drawn support from labor organizations, including UNITE HERE Local 25 and SEIU-1199.
 What does the District’s financial analysis say?
 The District’s Office of the Chief Financial Officer examined the potential financial effects of the proposal.
 The analysis acknowledges that higher minimum wages can increase earnings for lower-paid workers. But it also notes that businesses may respond to higher labor costs by raising prices for customers or reducing employment .
 The CFO’s office did not project a significant impact on District tax revenues, citing the possibility of several economic responses offsetting one another.
 In other words, the analysis recognizes potential benefits for workers while also acknowledging possible costs for businesses and consumers.
 Where does Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George stand?
 Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George has expressed support for phasing out the lower tipped minimum wage but has questioned the proposed jump to $25 an hour.
 In an interview with The Washington Sun, Lewis George said she believes the increase would be too abrupt given the District’s current economic pressures.
 “We’ve got some economic pressures right now, and raising the wages so abruptly without real thoughtful planning and understanding of how it would impact our economy — I believe that takes thoughtful planning but is not something that is practical and feasible right now,” Lewis George said. Through a spokesperson, Lewis George said that position remains unchanged.
 She also emphasized the need for a strategy that makes D.C. a better place to work and start a business while addressing the cost of housing, utilities and childcare.
 Could voters decide the issue next spring?
 Supporters of Initiative 87 submitted more than 43,600 petition signatures to the D.C. Board of Elections on November 12.
 The board must now verify the signatures to determine whether the proposal qualifies for the ballot.
 If certified, Initiative 87 could appear before voters during the District’s April 6, 2027 special election.
 The proposal would give D.C. voters another opportunity to weigh in on the District’s minimum wage and tipped-worker pay system, an issue that has been the subject of multiple ballot initiatives and legislative battles in recent years.
 For now, the future of the $25 minimum wage proposal rests with election officials and, potentially, District voters.
